Answer ALL questions: Section A is Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35) and Section B is Statistics (questions 36 to 50). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero for that question). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The scan is complete: cover page and the five pages of questions (pages 2 to 6), ending with "STOP, GO BACK AND CHECK YOUR WORK".

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

If $\dfrac{M}{x-1}+\dfrac{N}{x+2}\equiv\dfrac{2x-1}{(x-1)(x+2)}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply both sides by $(x-1)(x+2)$: $M(x+2)+N(x-1)\equiv 2x-1$. Put $x=1$: $3M=1$, so $M=\dfrac13$. Put $x=-2$: $-3N=-5$, so $N=\dfrac53$. Check by comparing coefficients: the coefficient of $x$ gives $M+N=\dfrac13+\dfrac53=2$ and the constant term gives $2M-N=\dfrac23-\dfrac53=-1$, both correct. Option A has the wrong sign for $N$ (a slip when substituting $x=-2$); options C and D fail $M+N=2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x+2},\ x\ne-2$, the range of $f$ does not include the element
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $y=\dfrac{x+1}{x+2}=1-\dfrac{1}{x+2}$. Since $\dfrac{1}{x+2}$ is never $0$, $y$ can never equal $1$; every other real value is attained (solving $y(x+2)=x+1$ gives $x=\dfrac{1-2y}{y-1}$, defined for every $y\ne1$). So the only value missing from the range is $1$. The value $-2$ (option C) is excluded from the DOMAIN, not from the range; the values $-1$ and $2$ are attained, for example $f\left(-\tfrac32\right)=-1$ and $f(-3)=2$. (Strictly $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is not defined at $x=-2$; the question intends the natural domain $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-2\}$.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The values of $x$ which satisfy the equation $2^{2x}-5\left(2^{x+1}\right)+2^4=0$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $2^{x+1}=2\cdot2^x$ and $2^4=16$, the equation is $(2^x)^2-10\cdot2^x+16=0$. Let $t=2^x>0$: $t^2-10t+16=0$, so $(t-2)(t-8)=0$ and $t=2$ or $t=8$. Hence $2^x=2$ gives $x=1$ and $2^x=8$ gives $x=3$. Check: $x=1$: $4-20+16=0$; $x=3$: $64-80+16=0$. Negative values of $x$ (options B, C, D) would need $2^x=2^{-1}$ or $2^{-3}$, which are not roots of the quadratic in $t$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution of the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x$, given that $y=1$ when $x=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The variables separate: $\int y\,dy=\int3x\,dx$, so $\dfrac{y^2}{2}=\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+c$, i.e. $y^2=3x^2+C$ with $C=2c$. Using $y=1$ at $x=1$: $1=3+C$, so $C=-2$ and $y^2=3x^2-2$. Check: differentiating $y^2=3x^2-2$ gives $2y\,y'=6x$, i.e. $y\,y'=3x$, and $y(1)^2=1$. At $x=1$ the other options give $y^2=4$, $2$ and $5$ (options B, C, D), so they do not satisfy $y(1)=1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In the set $A=\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$, a relation $\mathcal{R}$ is defined by $x\mathcal{R}y\Leftrightarrow x$ and $y$ have the same remainder when divided by $3$. The equivalence class of $3$, $[3]$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: The remainders on division by $3$ are: $0\to0$, $1\to1$, $2\to2$, $3\to0$, $4\to1$, $5\to2$, $6\to0$, $7\to1$. The number $3$ has remainder $0$, so $[3]=\{y\in A: y \text{ has remainder } 0\}=\{0,3,6\}$ (note that $0$ belongs to $A$). Option A forgets $0$; option B is $[1]=\{1,4,7\}$; option C is $[2]=\{2,5\}$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line segment $PQ$, where $P$ is the point $(2,4)$ and $Q$ is the point $(8,10)$, is the diameter of a circle. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown: A point $R(x,y)$ lies on the circle with diameter $PQ$ exactly when $\angle PRQ=90^\circ$, i.e. $\vec{RP}\cdot\vec{RQ}=0$: $(x-2)(x-8)+(y-4)(y-10)=0$. Check by expanding: $x^2-10x+16+y^2-14y+40=0$, i.e. $(x-5)^2+(y-7)^2=18$, a circle with centre $(5,7)$ (the midpoint of $PQ$) and radius $\sqrt{18}$ (half of $PQ=\sqrt{72}$). Both $P$ and $Q$ satisfy the equation. The other options mix the coordinates of $P$ and $Q$ or change signs, so $P$ and $Q$ do not lie on them. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When $f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6$ is divided by $2x+1$, the remainder is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $2x+1$ is $f\left(-\tfrac12\right)=2\left(-\tfrac18\right)+\tfrac14+\tfrac{13}{2}+6=-\tfrac14+\tfrac14+6.5+6=12.5$. The trap is option A: $f\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14+\tfrac14-6.5+6=0$ (so $2x-1$ is a factor), which comes from substituting $x=+\tfrac12$ instead of the root $x=-\tfrac12$ of $2x+1$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $|x-4|\ge2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $|x-4|\ge2$ means $x-4\ge2$ or $x-4\le-2$, i.e. $x\ge6$ or $x\le2$. On the number line these are the points at distance at least $2$ from $4$. Options A and B each keep only part of the answer with a wrong boundary; option C, $2\le x\le6$, is the solution of $|x-4|\le2$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $p$ and $q$ are two statements, then the contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The contrapositive of $p\Rightarrow q$ is $\sim q\Rightarrow\sim p$; it is logically equivalent to $p\Rightarrow q$ (if $q$ is false then $p$ cannot be true). Option A is the converse $q\Rightarrow p$ and option C is the inverse $\sim p\Rightarrow\sim q$; neither is equivalent to the original statement. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(x)=\begin{vmatrix}0&2&x^2\\0&1&x^2\\1&3x&2x^2\end{vmatrix}$, $f'(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand along the first column: only the entry $1$ in row 3 is non-zero, and its cofactor sign is $(-1)^{3+1}=+1$. So $f(x)=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}2&x^2\\1&x^2\end{vmatrix}=2x^2-x^2=x^2$. Hence $f'(x)=2x$. (Check at $x=1$: the determinant is $0\cdot(\dots)-2\cdot(0-1)+1\cdot(0-1)=2-1=1=1^2$.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f$ is a periodic function of period $4$ and that $f(x)=\begin{cases}9-x^2,&0<x\le2\\3x-1,&2<x\le4\end{cases}$, $f(19)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Periodicity of period $4$ gives $f(x+4k)=f(x)$, so $f(19)=f(19-4\cdot4)=f(3)$. Since $2<3\le4$, the second branch applies: $f(3)=3(3)-1=8$. Distractors: option A, $3\cdot19-1=56$, and option B, $9-19^2=-352$, plug $19$ straight into a branch without using the period; option C, $9-3^2=0$, uses the wrong branch for $x=3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The volume generated when the area of the finite region enclosed by the $x$ - axis and the curve $y=1-x^2$ is rotated completely about the $x$ - axis is
questions.corrige_markdown: The curve $y=1-x^2$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=\pm1$, so the region lies over $-1\le x\le1$. Rotating about the $x$-axis, the disc method gives $V=\pi\int_{-1}^{1}y^2\,dx=\pi\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x^2)^2\,dx=\dfrac{16\pi}{15}$. Option A integrates over $[0,1]$ only (half the solid, $\tfrac{8\pi}{15}$); option B doubles the integral ($\tfrac{32\pi}{15}$) although it already covers both halves (the factor $2\pi$ belongs to the shell method); option D omits the square. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
If a root of an equation $f(x)=0$ lies between $0$ and $1$, then

*Options as printed:* A) $f(0)f(1)\le0$   B) $f(0)f(1)>0$   C) $f(0)f(1)\ge0$   D) $f(0)f(1)<0$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The intended test is the sign-change criterion (intermediate value theorem): for a continuous $f$, a root in $(0,1)$ is located by $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ having opposite signs, i.e. $f(0)f(1)<0$ (option D); options B and C describe the same sign, i.e. no sign change. Strictly, however, the statement as worded does not imply any of the printed options: the converse of the theorem is false (for example $f(x)=\left(x-\tfrac12\right)^2$ has a root at $\tfrac12$ but $f(0)f(1)=\tfrac1{16}>0$), and option A, $f(0)f(1)\le0$, is equally compatible with the sign-change idea (it only adds the case of a root at an end point).

**Intended answer: D ($f(0)f(1)<0$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are such that $|\mathbf{p}|=3$, $|\mathbf{q}|=5$ and $\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}=-14$. The value of $|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}|=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Expand the square of the modulus: $|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}|^2=(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q})\cdot(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q})=|\mathbf{p}|^2-2\,\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}+|\mathbf{q}|^2=9-2(-14)+25=9+28+25=62$. Therefore $|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}|=\sqrt{62}$. Option D, $62$, is $|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}|^2$ (the square root has not been taken). (Consistency: $|\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q}|=14\le|\mathbf{p}||\mathbf{q}|=15$, so such vectors exist.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is given by $S_n=2n^2+n$. The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of the sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown: The $n$th term is $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$ for $n\ge2$, and $u_1=S_1$. Now $S_{n-1}=2(n-1)^2+(n-1)=2n^2-4n+2+n-1=2n^2-3n+1$, so $u_n=(2n^2+n)-(2n^2-3n+1)=4n-1$. For $n=1$ the formula gives $3=S_1$, so it holds for every $n\ge1$ (an arithmetic progression with $a=3$, $d=4$). Check with $n=2$: $u_2=S_2-S_1=10-3=7=4(2)-1$; option A would give $9$ and option C would give $9$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The expansion of $(3+5x)^{-2}$ is valid when
questions.corrige_markdown: Factor out the constant: $(3+5x)^{-2}=3^{-2}\left(1+\dfrac{5x}{3}\right)^{-2}$. The binomial series for a non-positive-integer index converges only when $\left|\dfrac{5x}{3}\right|<1$, i.e. $-\dfrac35<x<\dfrac35$. At the end points the terms $(-1)^k(k+1)\left(\tfrac{5x}{3}\right)^k$ do not tend to $0$, so the series diverges and the end points must be excluded (options A, C, D include at least one of them). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the curve with parametric equation $x=2t$, $y=\dfrac2t$, where $t$ is a parameter, is
questions.corrige_markdown: Eliminate $t$: from $x=2t$, $t=\dfrac x2$. Then $y=\dfrac2t=\dfrac{2}{x/2}=\dfrac4x$ (for $x\ne0$), i.e. $xy=4$, a rectangular hyperbola. Check with $t=1$: $(x,y)=(2,2)$ and $\dfrac42=2$. Option B, $y=\dfrac1x$, forgets the factor $2$ in $x=2t$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\left(\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Direct substitution gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac00$, so factorise: $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1$ for $x\ne1$. Hence the limit is $1+1=2$ (the function has a removable discontinuity at $x=1$). Option C, $0$, is the numerator evaluated at $x=1$ alone. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\dfrac18+\dfrac1{16}+\dots=$
questions.corrige_markdown: This is a geometric series with first term $a=\dfrac12$ and common ratio $r=\dfrac12$, with $|r|<1$, so it converges to $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}=\dfrac{1/2}{1/2}=1$. Check: the partial sums are $1-\dfrac1{2^n}$, which tend to $1$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The asymptotes of the curve $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2-5x+6}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Factorise the denominator: $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$. It vanishes at $x=2$ and $x=3$ while the numerator is $1$, so $x=2$ and $x=3$ are vertical asymptotes. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $y\to0$ (the degree of the numerator is less than that of the denominator), so $y=0$ is the horizontal asymptote. Options A and C use $x=-2,-3$ (sign error in the factorisation); option D claims $y=1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $y$ corresponding to some values of $x$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 18 | 21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 0.3 | 0.8 | $a$ | 2.1 | 3.0 | 4.3 |

Using the trapezium rule, $\displaystyle\int_6^{21}y\,dx\approx28.8$. The value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $6$ ordinates, hence $5$ strips of width $h=3$. The trapezium rule gives $\displaystyle\int_6^{21}y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\left[y_0+y_5+2(y_1+y_2+y_3+y_4)\right]=\dfrac32\left[0.3+4.3+2(0.8+a+2.1+3.0)\right]$. The bracket is $4.6+2(5.9+a)=16.4+2a$, so the estimate is $\dfrac32(16.4+2a)=24.6+3a$. Setting $24.6+3a=28.8$ gives $3a=4.2$, so $a=1.4$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The gradient of the implicit function $2x+xy=5$ at the point $(1,1)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, using the product rule on $xy$: $2+y+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2+y}{x}$.

At $(1,1)$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2+1}{1}=-3$.

Note: the point $(1,1)$ does not lie exactly on the curve ($2\cdot1+1\cdot1=3\neq5$); the question is answered by evaluating the derivative formula at the given coordinates, which is the only reading that gives one of the options.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\sin35^\circ+\sin25^\circ=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Use the sum-to-product formula $\sin A+\sin B=2\sin\dfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\dfrac{A-B}{2}$ with $A=35^\circ$, $B=25^\circ$: $\sin35^\circ+\sin25^\circ=2\sin30^\circ\cos5^\circ=2\cdot\dfrac12\cos5^\circ=\cos5^\circ$. Numerically both sides are $0.99619$. Option A forgets that $\sin30^\circ=\dfrac12$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the plane $\mu x-2y+5z=6$ and the line $\mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}+s(\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k})$ are parallel, the value of the constant $\mu$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: The plane has normal vector $\mathbf{n}=\begin{pmatrix}\mu\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and the line has direction $\mathbf{d}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}$. A line is parallel to a plane when its direction is perpendicular to the normal: $\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{d}=0$, i.e. $\mu+4+15=0$, so $\mu=-19$. Check that the line is not inside the plane: the point $(2,-3,1)$ gives $-19(2)+6+5=-27\ne6$, so the line is parallel to the plane and not contained in it. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $u=2+3x^2$, so $du=6x\,dx$ and $x\,dx=\dfrac{du}{6}$. Then $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}\,dx=\dfrac16\int\dfrac{du}{u}=\dfrac16\ln|u|+K=\dfrac16\ln(2+3x^2)+K$ (the argument is always positive). Check: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\dfrac16\ln(2+3x^2)\right]=\dfrac16\cdot\dfrac{6x}{2+3x^2}=\dfrac{x}{2+3x^2}$. Option A forgets the factor $\dfrac16$; option B multiplies by $6$ instead of dividing. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\cos\left(2x+\dfrac\pi3\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\dfrac{\sqrt3}2=\cos\dfrac\pi6$, the equation $\cos\theta=\cos\alpha$ has the general solution $\theta=2n\pi\pm\alpha$ ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$). With $\theta=2x+\dfrac\pi3$ and $\alpha=\dfrac\pi6$: $2x+\dfrac\pi3=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6$, so $2x=2n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi6-\dfrac\pi3$. Check: with the plus sign, $2x=2n\pi-\dfrac\pi6$ and $\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi6+\dfrac\pi3\right)=\cos\dfrac\pi6$; with the minus sign, $2x=2n\pi-\dfrac\pi2$ and $\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi2+\dfrac\pi3\right)=\cos\left(-\dfrac\pi6\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$. Option B keeps only the plus sign and so loses half of the solutions. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the line $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+6\mathbf{k}+\mu(-5\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k})$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The line passes through the point $(1,-1,6)$ with direction vector $(-5,1,-4)$. Its Cartesian form is $\dfrac{x-1}{-5}=\dfrac{y-(-1)}{1}=\dfrac{z-6}{-4}$, i.e. $\dfrac{x-1}{-5}=\dfrac{y+1}{1}=\dfrac{z-6}{-4}$. Check: $\mu=1$ gives $(-4,0,2)$ and $\dfrac{-5}{-5}=\dfrac{1}{1}=\dfrac{-4}{-4}=1$. Options A and B swap the roles of the position vector and the direction vector; option D uses the point $(-1,1,-6)$ (signs of the point reversed). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the sequence $u_n$, where $n\in\mathbb{N}$, is strictly monotonic increasing then
questions.corrige_markdown: A sequence is strictly increasing when each term is strictly larger than the previous one: $u_{n+1}>u_n$ for every $n$. Option A describes a strictly decreasing sequence, B a decreasing (non-strict) one, and D a (non-strict) increasing sequence, which allows equal consecutive terms. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A bijective function is that which is
questions.corrige_markdown: A function is bijective when it is both injective (one-to-one: different inputs give different outputs) and surjective (onto: every element of the codomain is an image). Option A describes an equivalence relation; option C (injective, surjective and anti-symmetric) mixes the properties of functions with those of relations (anti-symmetry belongs to order relations); option D is about sequences. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z=1+i$ can be expressed in exponential form as
questions.corrige_markdown: The modulus is $|z|=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$ and the argument is $\arg z=\arctan\dfrac11=\dfrac\pi4$ ($z$ is in the first quadrant). So $z=\sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}$. Check: $\sqrt2\left(\cos\dfrac\pi4+i\sin\dfrac\pi4\right)=\sqrt2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt2}2+i\dfrac{\sqrt2}2\right)=1+i$. Option A omits the modulus; option B has the wrong argument; option D has the wrong modulus. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{\cos5\theta+i\sin5\theta}{(\cos2\theta+i\sin2\theta)^{-3}}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: By de Moivre's theorem $\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta=e^{in\theta}$. The numerator is $e^{5i\theta}$ and the denominator is $(e^{2i\theta})^{-3}=e^{-6i\theta}$. Dividing by $e^{-6i\theta}$ is multiplying by $e^{6i\theta}$, so the quotient is $e^{5i\theta}\cdot e^{6i\theta}=e^{11i\theta}=\cos11\theta+i\sin11\theta$. Option A comes from adding $5\theta+2\theta$ and ignoring the power $-3$; option B ($e^{-i\theta}$) comes from $5\theta-6\theta$, i.e. forgetting that dividing by a negative power adds the angle. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Suppose $f(0.6)=0.7$ and $f'(0.6)=10.6$. If $x_1=0.6$ is the first approximation to the root of $f(x)=0$, then using Newton Raphson method, a second approximate root $x_2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The Newton-Raphson iteration is $x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. With $x_1=0.6$: $x_2=0.6-\dfrac{0.7}{10.6}\approx0.534$. Options A and B add the correction instead of subtracting it; options B and D use the inverted ratio $\dfrac{f'}{f}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given the matrix $A$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&3&1\\0&-1&4\end{pmatrix}$, the determinant of $A^T$, where $A^T$ is the transpose of $A$, is
questions.corrige_markdown: A matrix and its transpose have the same determinant, so $\det A^T=\det A$. Expand $\det A$ along the first column, whose only non-zero entry is $1$: $\det A=1\cdot\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\-1&4\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot4-1\cdot(-1)=12+1=13$. Hence $\det A^T=13$. Option A, $12$, forgets the term $-1\cdot1$ with its sign. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The image of the line $y=3x$ under the transformation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ is the line
questions.corrige_markdown: A general point of the line is $(x,3x)$. Its image is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\3x\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2x+3x\\x+9x\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5x\\10x\end{pmatrix}$. The image point $(X,Y)=(5x,10x)$ satisfies $Y=2X$, so the image line is $y=2x$. Option C writes the slope $\dfrac5{10}$ the wrong way round (it is the ratio $X:Y$ rather than $Y:X$). **Answer: D.**

questions.corrige_markdown: In the diagram the shaded region is the part of the circle $A$ that lies outside the circle $B$ (the lens where the two circles overlap is white, and nothing of $B$ outside $A$ is shaded). Points in $A$ and not in $B$ are $A\cap B'$. The other options: $A'\cap(A\cap B)$ and $B'\cap(A\cap B)$ are both empty (a point cannot be in $A\cap B$ and outside $A$ or outside $B$), and $A'\cap B$ is the part of $B$ outside $A$ (the unshaded crescent on the right). **Answer: C.**

If a data set is such that $n=100$, $\sum x=2900$ and $\sum x^2=846900$, then $\mathrm{Var}(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The mean is $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum x}{n}=\dfrac{2900}{100}=29$. The variance (divisor $n$) is $\mathrm{Var}(x)=\dfrac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2=\dfrac{846900}{100}-29^2=8469-841=7628$. The distractors are built from this calculation: option B, $87.34=\sqrt{7628}$, is the standard deviation; option C, $8440=8469-29$, subtracts the mean instead of its square; option D, $91.87=\sqrt{8440}$, is the square root of option C. (With divisor $n-1=99$ the unbiased estimate would be $7705.05$, which is not offered, so the divisor $n$ is intended.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The mean of $40$ numbers is $10$. If $10$ of the $40$ numbers have a mean of $4$, then the mean of the remaining $30$ numbers is
questions.corrige_markdown: Total of all $40$ numbers: $40\times10=400$. Total of the $10$ numbers: $10\times4=40$. Total of the remaining $30$ numbers: $400-40=360$, so their mean is $\dfrac{360}{30}=12$. Check: $\dfrac{10\cdot4+30\cdot12}{40}=\dfrac{400}{40}=10$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For a negatively skewed distribution,
questions.corrige_markdown: A negatively skewed distribution has a long tail on the left (towards small values). The mode is at the peak (the largest of the three), the extreme small values pull the mean furthest to the left, and the median lies between them: $\text{Mean}<\text{Median}<\text{Mode}$. (For a positively skewed distribution the inequalities are reversed: Mode $<$ Median $<$ Mean, which is option D.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A)=\dfrac15$, $P(B)=\dfrac34$, and $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac7{10}$. $P(A\cap B)=$

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac12$   B) $\dfrac{19}{20}$   C) $\dfrac15$   D) $\dfrac14$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The addition rule gives $P(A\cap B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B)=\dfrac15+\dfrac34-\dfrac7{10}=\dfrac{4+15-14}{20}=\dfrac5{20}=\dfrac14$, which is option D. However the printed data are inconsistent, so no event pair can have these probabilities: a union cannot be smaller than one of its events, yet $P(A\cup B)=\dfrac7{10}<P(B)=\dfrac34$; equivalently $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac14$ would exceed $P(A)=\dfrac15$, which is impossible for an intersection. The formula applied mechanically gives $\dfrac14$ (option D).

**Intended answer: D ($\dfrac14$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The discrete random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | $\dfrac1{14}$ | $a$ | $\dfrac3{14}$ |

The value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The probabilities of a discrete distribution sum to $1$: $\dfrac1{14}+a+\dfrac3{14}=1$, so $a=1-\dfrac4{14}=\dfrac{10}{14}\left(=\dfrac57\right)$, which lies between $0$ and $1$ as required. Option B, $\dfrac{11}{14}$, forgets the $\dfrac1{14}$; option C, $\dfrac4{14}$, is the sum of the two given probabilities. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables such that $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(3,0.2)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(5,0.2)$, the distribution of $X+Y$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $X$ counts the successes in $3$ independent trials and $Y$ the successes in $5$ other independent trials, all with the same success probability $0.2$. Hence $X+Y$ counts the successes in $3+5=8$ independent trials of probability $0.2$: $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(8,0.2)$. (Check with the mean: $E(X+Y)=0.6+1.0=1.6=8\times0.2$.) The number of trials adds but the probability stays the same; adding probabilities (option A) or squaring them (B, D) is wrong. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(3.4)$, then the most likely value or the mode of $X$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a Poisson distribution $\dfrac{P(X=k)}{P(X=k-1)}=\dfrac{\lambda}{k}$, which is greater than $1$ exactly when $k<\lambda=3.4$. So the probabilities increase up to $k=3$ and decrease from $k=4$ onwards: the mode is $\lfloor3.4\rfloor=3$. Check: $P(X=2)=0.1929$, $P(X=3)=0.2186$, $P(X=4)=0.1858$. There are two modes ($\lambda-1$ and $\lambda$) only when $\lambda$ is an integer, which is not the case here (options B and D). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable $X$ is defined as “the number of tosses of a coin until a head is obtained”. $E(X)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $X$ follows a geometric distribution with success probability $p$ (the probability of a head), $P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$ for $k=1,2,\dots$, and $E(X)=\dfrac1p$. The printed question does not give $p$, so a fair coin is assumed: $p=\dfrac12$ and $E(X)=2$. Direct check: $E(X)=\sum_{k\ge1}k\left(\dfrac12\right)^k=2$. Option A would be the case of a coin that always shows a head; options C and D are not valid expectations of a count that is at least $1$ (an expectation of a variable taking the values $1,2,3,\dots$ cannot be below $1$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A continuous random variable, $X$, has a probability density function defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}m(2x+3),&0\le x\le2\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ The value of the constant $m$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: A probability density function integrates to $1$: $\displaystyle\int_0^2m(2x+3)\,dx=m\left[x^2+3x\right]_0^2=m(4+6)=10m=1$, so $m=\dfrac1{10}$. Check: $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+3}{10}\ge0$ on $[0,2]$ and the total area is $\dfrac{10}{10}=1$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A continuous random variable, $X$, has a probability density function defined by $f(x)=3e^{-3x}$ for $x\ge0$. The expected value, $E(X)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $E(X)=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty x\cdot3e^{-3x}\,dx$. Integrate by parts with $u=x$, $dv=3e^{-3x}dx$: $E(X)=\left[-xe^{-3x}\right]_0^\infty+\int_0^\infty e^{-3x}\,dx=0+\left[-\dfrac13e^{-3x}\right]_0^\infty=\dfrac13$. This is an exponential distribution with rate $\lambda=3$, whose mean is $\dfrac1\lambda=\dfrac13$. Option B is the rate itself; the negative values A and C are impossible because $X\ge0$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The heights of some maize plants in a farm are normally distributed with a mean of $130$ cm and a standard deviation of $4$ cm. The probability that a randomly chosen plant has a height less than $140$ cm is
questions.corrige_markdown: Standardise: $Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}=\dfrac{140-130}{4}=2.5$, so $P(X<140)=P(Z<2.5)=\Phi(2.5)\approx0.9938$. Option A, $\Phi(-2.5)$, is $P(X<120)$; option C, $1-2\Phi(-2.5)=0.9876$, is the two-sided probability $P(120<X<140)$; option D, $1-2\Phi(2.5)\approx-0.9876$, is negative and so cannot be a probability. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X\sim N(40,4)$ and $Y\sim N(60,9)$, the distribution of $3Y-2X$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Here $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is used, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=9$; $X$ and $Y$ are taken to be independent (the printed question does not say so, but it is needed). A linear combination of independent normal variables is normal. Mean: $E(3Y-2X)=3(60)-2(40)=100$. Variance: $\mathrm{Var}(3Y-2X)=3^2\mathrm{Var}(Y)+(-2)^2\mathrm{Var}(X)=9\cdot9+4\cdot4=81+16=97$. So $3Y-2X\sim N(100,97)$. The distractors come from subtracting variances ($81-16=65$, option D), forgetting to square the coefficients ($27-8=19$, option B, and $27+8=35$, option A). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The masses of the teachers in a certain college can be modeled by a normal distribution with mean $70$ kg and standard deviation $5$ kg. If $4$ teachers are chosen at random then the distribution of the sample mean is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a sample of size $n$ from $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ the sample mean satisfies $\bar X\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$: the mean is unchanged and the VARIANCE is divided by $n$. With $\mu=70$, $\sigma=5$, $n=4$: $\bar X\sim N\left(70,\dfrac{5^2}{4}\right)=N(70,6.25)$ (standard error $2.5$ kg). Options A and B change the mean; option C divides the standard deviation (not the variance) by $4$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In a hypothesis test where $H_0$ is the null hypothesis and $H_1$ is the alternative hypothesis, a type II error is committed when
questions.corrige_markdown: A type II error is a failure to detect a false null hypothesis: $H_0$ is NOT rejected although $H_0$ is false (equivalently, $H_1$ is true). Option A is a type I error (rejecting a true $H_0$); option B is a correct decision; option D, rejecting $H_0$ when $H_1$ is false (i.e. when $H_0$ is true), is again a type I error. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For a data set, the regression lines of $Y$ on $X$ and $X$ on $Y$ are $y=0.5x-0.3$ and $x=0.7y-0.11$ respectively. The product-moment correlation coefficient for these data is
questions.corrige_markdown: The slope of the regression line of $Y$ on $X$ is $b_{yx}=r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}=0.5$ and that of $X$ on $Y$ is $b_{xy}=r\dfrac{s_x}{s_y}=0.7$. Their product is $b_{yx}b_{xy}=r^2=0.5\times0.7=0.35$, so $|r|=\sqrt{0.35}\approx0.592$ (a valid value since $r^2\le1$). Both regression coefficients are positive, and $r$ has the same sign as them, so $r=+\sqrt{0.35}$. Option A, $\sqrt{0.033}$, is built from the intercepts ($0.3\times0.11$) which play no role; options B and D have the wrong sign. **Answer: C.**
